analysis.one_liner: Repeals five federal tax breaks for the largest oil companies and Gulf of Mexico royalty relief, directing savings to deficit reduction.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 23 Senate Democrats, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end several long-standing tax deductions used by the biggest oil companies — including deductions for foreign taxes paid, for domestic oil production, for drilling costs, for oil well depletion, and for chemicals injected into old wells to squeeze out more oil. It would also repeal royalty relief that lets some companies drill in deep Gulf of Mexico waters while paying reduced or no royalties to the government. All the money saved would go to reducing the federal deficit or debt. The bill was introduced in August 2017, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and no action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, since the roughly several-billion-per-year cost of these tax breaks would end and the savings would be deposited in the Treasury for deficit reduction. Future generations also benefit from a smaller federal debt. Ordinary people do not receive any direct payment — the benefit comes through reduced government borrowing.

how_it_helps.text: Ends five tax benefits available only to major integrated oil companies — companies with over $1 billion in annual gross receipts and at least 500,000 barrels of daily worldwide oil production — while leaving smaller producers' treatment largely intact.

Repeals 2005-era royalty relief that suspended royalties owed to the federal government for deep gas wells in shallow Gulf waters and deepwater production in the Western and Central Gulf, meaning those leases pay what the oil is actually worth.
Requires that all net savings be deposited in the Treasury and used to reduce the federal budget deficit or debt, so the money cannot be spent elsewhere.

analysis.who_pays: Major integrated oil companies, which would lose the deductions and pay full Gulf royalties. Some portion of the lost tax benefits could show up as somewhat higher fuel prices if companies pass costs through to consumers.

drawbacks.text: Companies facing higher tax bills can pass some of the cost to consumers through higher gasoline and heating prices, so households could see modestly higher energy costs.
The savings go entirely to deficit reduction, not to any direct benefit for households, so the visible payoff for ordinary people is indirect.

Supporters of these deductions argue the domestic production deduction and drilling cost deductions encourage investment and keep domestic energy production strong; the bill targets only the largest companies but still narrows those incentives.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: the largest oil companies give up tax breaks that smaller firms keep, the government collects full royalties on Gulf leases, and the money reduces the deficit. The cost to households, if any, would likely be modest and spread across fuel prices, while the fiscal benefit is real but indirect. The bill is narrowly drawn and does not raise taxes on smaller producers, which makes the design targeted rather than sweeping.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in August 2017, and the committee never acted on it, so the bill died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Menendez introduced the bill on August 2, 2017, with 22 Democratic cosponsors joining on introduction.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
The Finance Committee held no markup, reported no vote, and the bill never reached the Senate floor; its last recorded action was the referral on the day of introduction.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies kept all five tax benefits and the Gulf royalty relief remained in place, because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies, which kept every tax benefit

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee and Senate majority took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would end five federal tax deductions available to companies with over $1 billion in gross receipts and 500,000 barrels of daily production, and close a successor-company loophole so reorganizations cannot escape the definition. These companies benefit from the current tax code at public expense; their gain under the status quo is revenue the Treasury does not collect.

industries.industry: Gulf of Mexico deepwater and deep-gas producers
industries.note: The bill repeals 2005 royalty relief that suspended the royalties these producers owe on federal leases, so they would begin paying full value for publicly owned oil and gas. The bill never passed, so the relief remained in effect.
Savings from the repealed breaks and restored royalties must be deposited in the Treasury for deficit or debt reduction, reducing the borrowing burden that falls on households.
